arXiv:1810.06909v1 [math.AP] 16 Oct 2018

Global bounded and unbounded solutions to a chemotaxis system with indirect signal production

Philippe Laurençot Address: Institut de Mathématiques de Toulouse, UMR 5219, Université de Toulouse, CNRS
F–31062 Toulouse Cedex 9, France Email address: laurenco@math.univ-toulouse.fr
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

The well-posedness of a chemotaxis system with indirect signal production in a two-dimensional domain is shown, all solutions being global unlike the classical Keller-Segel chemotaxis system. Nevertheless, there is a threshold value McM_{c} of the mass of the first component which separates two different behaviours: solutions are bounded when the mass is below McM_{c} while there are unbounded solutions starting from initial conditions having a mass exceeding McM_{c}. This result extends to arbitrary two-dimensional domains a previous result of Tao & Winkler (2017) obtained for radially symmetric solutions to a simplified version of the model in a ball and relies on a different approach involving a Liapunov functional.

Key words and phrases: 
chemotaxis system - global existence - boundedness - unbounded global solutions
1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
35B40 - 35M33 - 35K10 - 35Q92

1. Introduction

Chemotaxis models have been derived in [19, 21, 24] to describe the spreading and aggregative behaviour of the mountain pine beetle which has a major impact on the forest industry in North America. These models describe the space and time evolution of the density uu of flying beetles, the density vv of nesting beetles, and the concentration ww of beetle pheromone (chemoattractant). The main behavioural difference between flying and nesting beetles is that the latter do not disperse in space while the former move randomly in space, their motion being biased by high gradients of the pheromone concentration. A very important feature in the model is that the pheromone is produced by the nesting beetles and not by the flying ones, though it influences only the motion of the latter. This is in sharp contrast with the classical Keller-Segel model where the chemical inducing a bias in the motion of the species is produced directly by the species itself. As we shall see below, this feature alters significantly the dynamics, at least in two space dimensions.

A simplified version of the models derived in [19, 21, 24] is considered in [23] and reads

(1.1a) ∂tu\displaystyle\partial_{t}u =div(∇u−u∇w) in (0,∞)×Ω,\displaystyle=\mathrm{div}\left(\nabla u-u\nabla w\right)\;\;\text{ in }\;\;(0,\infty)\times\Omega\ ,
(1.1b) ν​ε​∂tv\displaystyle\nu\varepsilon\partial_{t}v =u−v​ in ​(0,∞)×Ω,\displaystyle=u-v\;\;\text{ in }\;\;(0,\infty)\times\Omega\ ,
(1.1c) 0\displaystyle 0 =D​Δ​w−⟨v⟩+v​ in ​(0,∞)×Ω,\displaystyle=D\Delta w-\langle v\rangle+v\;\;\text{ in }\;\;(0,\infty)\times\Omega\ ,
supplemented with no-flux boundary conditions for uu and ww
(1.1d) ∇u⋅𝐧=∇w⋅𝐧=0 on (0,∞)×∂Ω,\nabla u\cdot\mathbf{n}=\nabla w\cdot\mathbf{n}=0\;\;\text{ on }\;\;(0,\infty)\times\partial\Omega\ ,
the normalization condition for ww
(1.1e) ⟨w⟩=0​ in ​(0,∞),\langle w\rangle=0\;\;\text{ in }\;\;(0,\infty)\ ,

and non-negative initial conditions (ui​n,vi​n)(u^{in},v^{in}) for (u,v)(u,v). Here Ω\Omega is a smooth bounded domain of ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, ν\nu, ε\varepsilon, and DD are positive parameters, and ⟨v⟩\langle v\rangle in (1.1c) and ⟨w⟩\langle w\rangle in (1.1e) denote the mean value with respect to the space variable of vv and ww, respectively. Recall that, for z∈L1​(Ω)z\in L^{1}(\Omega), its mean value is given by

⟨z⟩:=1|Ω|​∫Ωz⁡(x)​𝑑x.\langle z\rangle:=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}z(x)\ \mathrm{d}x\ .

A Jäger-Luckhaus version of the Keller-Segel chemotaxis system [14] is recovered from (1.1) by setting ν​ε=0\nu\varepsilon=0 and reads, since v=uv=u in that case,

(1.2a) ∂tu\displaystyle\partial_{t}u =div(∇u−u∇w) in (0,∞)×Ω,\displaystyle=\mathrm{div}\left(\nabla u-u\nabla w\right)\;\;\text{ in }\;\;(0,\infty)\times\Omega\ ,
(1.2b) 0\displaystyle 0 =D​Δ​w−⟨u⟩+u​ in ​(0,∞)×Ω,\displaystyle=D\Delta w-\langle u\rangle+u\;\;\text{ in }\;\;(0,\infty)\times\Omega\ ,
supplemented with no-flux boundary conditions for uu and ww
(1.2c) ∇u⋅𝐧=∇w⋅𝐧=0 on (0,∞)×∂Ω,\nabla u\cdot\mathbf{n}=\nabla w\cdot\mathbf{n}=0\;\;\text{ on }\;\;(0,\infty)\times\partial\Omega\ ,
the normalization condition for ww
(1.2d) ⟨w⟩=0​ in ​(0,∞),\langle w\rangle=0\;\;\text{ in }\;\;(0,\infty)\ ,

and a non-negative initial condition ui​nu^{in} for uu. Observe that, in (1.2), the chemoattractant is produced directly by the species with density uu, instead of being produced through another species as in (1.1). A first consequence of this feature is that all solutions to (1.1) are global [23, Theorem 1.1]. This global existence property contrasts markedly with the situation for (1.2) for which the following is known: solutions to (1.2) are global when either ‖ui​n‖1<4​π​D\|u^{in}\|_{1}<4\pi D or Ω\Omega is a ball, ui​nu^{in} is radially symmetric, and ‖ui​n‖1>8​π​D\|u^{in}\|_{1}>8\pi D [5, 14, 15]. Finite time blowup may take place when either ‖ui​n‖1>4​π​D\|u^{in}\|_{1}>4\pi D or Ω\Omega is a ball, ui​nu^{in} is radially symmetric, and ‖ui​n‖1>8​π​D\|u^{in}\|_{1}>8\pi D [14, 15, 16, 20], see also the survey [12].

A striking feature of the dynamics of (1.1), uncovered in [23], is that, though all solutions to (1.1) are global, a threshold phenomenon occurs in infinite time. More precisely, when Ω\Omega is a ball, say Ω=B1​(0):={x∈ℝ2:|x|<1}\Omega=B_{1}(0):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\ :\ |x|<1\}, and the initial conditions (ui​n,vi​n)(u^{in},v^{in}) are radially symmetric, so that the solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) of (1.1) is also radially symmetric for all times, it is shown in [23, Theorems 1.2 & 1.3] that all (radially symmetric) solutions are actually bounded when ‖ui​n‖1<8​π​D\|u^{in}\|_{1}<8\pi D while there are unbounded solutions emanating from initial conditions satisfying ‖ui​n‖1>8​π​D\|u^{in}\|_{1}>8\pi D, the L∞L^{\infty}-norm of u⁡(t)u(t) growing up as t→∞t\to\infty at an exponential rate. The approach of [23] exploits the classical fact that the specific structure of (1.1) and the radial symmetry of the solutions allow one to reduce (1.1) to a single nonlocal parabolic equation for the cumulative distribution function UU defined by

U⁡(t,|x|):=∫0|x|σ​u¯​(t,σ)​𝑑σ,(t,x)∈(0,∞)×B1​(0),U(t,|x|):=\int_{0}^{\sqrt{|x|}}\sigma\bar{u}(t,\sigma)\ \mathrm{d}\sigma\ ,\qquad(t,x)\in(0,\infty)\times B_{1}(0)\ ,

where u¯​(t,|x|):=u​(t,x)\bar{u}(t,|x|):=u(t,x) for (t,x)∈(0,∞)×B1​(0)(t,x)\in(0,\infty)\times B_{1}(0). Even though the parabolic equation solved by UU involves a nonlocal term, it turns out that such a powerful tool as the comparison principle becomes available, see [23, Lemma 4.2], and the proofs of [23, Theorems 1.2 & 1.3] rely on the construction of suitable supersolutions and subsolutions.

This technique is however restricted to (1.1) in a radially symmetric setting and does not allow one to handle more general initial conditions or to consider an arbitrary domain Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}. Neither does it extend to the version of (1.1) involving degradation of the chemoattractant

(1.3a) ∂tu\displaystyle\partial_{t}u =div(∇u−u∇w) in (0,∞)×Ω,\displaystyle=\mathrm{div}\left(\nabla u-u\nabla w\right)\;\;\text{ in }\;\;(0,\infty)\times\Omega\ ,
(1.3b) ν​ε​∂tv\displaystyle\nu\varepsilon\partial_{t}v =u−v​ in ​(0,∞)×Ω,\displaystyle=u-v\;\;\text{ in }\;\;(0,\infty)\times\Omega\ ,
(1.3c) 0\displaystyle 0 =D​Δ​w−δ​w+v​ in ​(0,∞)×Ω,\displaystyle=D\Delta w-\delta w+v\;\;\text{ in }\;\;(0,\infty)\times\Omega\ ,

with δ>0\delta>0, supplemented with no-flux boundary conditions for uu and ww and non-negative initial conditions (ui​n,vi​n)(u^{in},v^{in}) for (u,v)(u,v), nor to its parabolic counterpart

(1.4a) ∂tu\displaystyle\partial_{t}u =div(∇u−u∇w) in (0,∞)×Ω,\displaystyle=\mathrm{div}\left(\nabla u-u\nabla w\right)\;\;\text{ in }\;\;(0,\infty)\times\Omega\ ,
(1.4b) ν​ε​∂tv\displaystyle\nu\varepsilon\partial_{t}v =u−v​ in ​(0,∞)×Ω,\displaystyle=u-v\;\;\text{ in }\;\;(0,\infty)\times\Omega\ ,
(1.4c) ν​∂tw\displaystyle\nu\partial_{t}w =D​Δ​w−δ​w+v​ in ​(0,∞)×Ω,\displaystyle=D\Delta w-\delta w+v\;\;\text{ in }\;\;(0,\infty)\times\Omega\ ,
supplemented with no-flux boundary conditions for uu and ww
(1.4d) (∇u−u∇w)⋅𝐧=∇w⋅𝐧=0 on (0,∞)×∂Ω,\left(\nabla u-u\nabla w\right)\cdot\mathbf{n}=\nabla w\cdot\mathbf{n}=0\;\;\text{ on }\;\;(0,\infty)\times\partial\Omega\ ,

and initial conditions

(1.5) (u,v,w)​(0)=(ui​n,vi​n,wi​n)​ in ​Ω.(u,v,w)(0)=(u^{in},v^{in},w^{in})\;\;\text{ in }\;\;\Omega\ .

The main contribution of this paper is to show that the systems (1.1), (1.3), and (1.4) share the same infinite time threshold phenomenon uncovered in [23], without restrictions on the two-dimensional domain Ω\Omega and the initial data. This requires a different argument and we actually show that (1.1), (1.3), and (1.4) all possess a Liapunov functional, and that the properties of this Liapunov functional provide insight on the boundedness or unboundedness of the solutions.

From now on, we shall focus on (1.4)-(1.5) and will return briefly to (1.1) and (1.3) in Section 5. Introducing

(1.6) L⁡(r):=r​ln⁡r−r+1≥0,r≥0,L(r):=r\ln{r}-r+1\geq 0\ ,\qquad r\geq 0\ ,

and

(1.7a) ℰ0​(u,w)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{0}(u,w) :=∫Ω[L⁡(u)−u​w]​𝑑x+D2​‖∇w‖22+δ2​‖w‖22,\displaystyle:=\int_{\Omega}\left[L(u)-uw\right]\ \mathrm{d}x+\frac{D}{2}\|\nabla w\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{\delta}{2}\|w\|_{2}^{2}\ ,
(1.7b) ℰ⁡(u,v,w)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(u,v,w) :=ℰ0​(u,w)+ε2​‖−D​Δ​w+δ​w−v‖22,\displaystyle:=\mathcal{E}_{0}(u,w)+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\|-D\Delta w+\delta w-v\|_{2}^{2}\ ,

(1.8a) ∂tu\displaystyle\partial_{t}u =div(∇u−u∇w) in (0,∞)×Ω,\displaystyle=\mathrm{div}\left(\nabla u-u\nabla w\right)\;\;\text{ in }\;\;(0,\infty)\times\Omega\ ,
(1.8b) ν​∂tw\displaystyle\nu\partial_{t}w =D​Δ​w−δ​w+u​ in ​(0,∞)×Ω,\displaystyle=D\Delta w-\delta w+u\;\;\text{ in }\;\;(0,\infty)\times\Omega\ ,
(1.8c) ∇u⋅𝐧=∇w⋅𝐧=0 on (0,∞)×∂Ω,\displaystyle\nabla u\cdot\mathbf{n}=\nabla w\cdot\mathbf{n}=0\;\;\text{ on }\;\;(0,\infty)\times\partial\Omega\ ,
(1.8d) (u,w)​(0)=(ui​n,wi​n)​ in ​Ω,\displaystyle(u,w)(0)=(u^{in},w^{in})\;\;\text{ in }\;\;\Omega\ ,

and, as such, its properties have been thoroughly studied [9, 10, 11, 13, 17]. In particular, introducing the set

(1.9) 𝒜M:={(u,w)∈L1(Ω)×W21(Ω):u≥0,w≥0,∥u∥1=M}\mathcal{A}_{M}:=\left\{(u,w)\in L_{1}(\Omega)\times W_{2}^{1}(\Omega)\ :\ u\geq 0\ ,\ w\geq 0\ ,\ \|u\|_{1}=M\right\}

for M≥0M\geq 0, it is known that

(1.10) inf(u,w)∈𝒜Mℰ0​(u,w)>−∞ if M∈[0,4​π​D],inf(u,w)∈𝒜Mℰ0​(u,w)=−∞ if M>4​π​D,\begin{array}[]{lcl}\displaystyle{\inf_{(u,w)\in\mathcal{A}_{M}}\mathcal{E}_{0}(u,w)}>-\infty&\text{ if }&M\in[0,4\pi D]\ ,\\ \displaystyle{\inf_{(u,w)\in\mathcal{A}_{M}}\mathcal{E}_{0}(u,w)}=-\infty&\text{ if }&M>4\pi D\ ,\end{array}

a property which has far-reaching consequences on the dynamics of (1.8). Indeed, given M>0M>0, global existence and blowup of solutions to (1.8) are intimately related to the finiteness or not of the infimum of ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0} on 𝒜M\mathcal{A}_{M} [9, 10, 11, 13, 17]. As we shall see below, the property (1.10) also plays an important role in the dynamics of (1.4)-(1.5), a feature which is actually not so surprising as there is a close connection between (1.4)-(1.5) and (1.8). Indeed, (1.8) can formally be derived from (1.4)-(1.5) by setting ε=0\varepsilon=0.

We now describe our results on (1.4)-(1.5) and begin with its well-posedness. For θ∈(2/3,1)\theta\in(2/3,1) and M≥0M\geq 0, we set

Theorem 1.1.

Let θ∈(5/6,1)\theta\in(5/6,1) and consider initial conditions (ui​n,vi​n,wi​n)∈ℐM,θ(u^{in},v^{in},w^{in})\in\mathcal{I}_{M,\theta}. Then the system (1.4)-(1.5) has a unique non-negative weak solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) in W31W^{1}_{3} defined on [0,∞)[0,\infty) satisfying

u\displaystyle u ∈C⁡([0,∞),W3,ℬ2​θ​(Ω))∩C1​([0,∞),W3,ℬ2​θ−2​(Ω)),\displaystyle\in C([0,\infty);W_{3,\mathcal{B}}^{2\theta}(\Omega))\cap C^{1}([0,\infty);W^{2\theta-2}_{3,\mathcal{B}}(\Omega))\ ,
v\displaystyle v ∈C1​([0,∞),W31​(Ω)),\displaystyle\in C^{1}([0,\infty);W^{1}_{3}(\Omega))\ ,
w\displaystyle w ∈C⁡([0,∞),W3,ℬ2​(Ω))∩C1​([0,∞),L3​(Ω)),\displaystyle\in C([0,\infty);W_{3,\mathcal{B}}^{2}(\Omega))\cap C^{1}([0,\infty);L_{3}(\Omega))\ ,

and

(1.14) ‖u⁡(t)‖1=M:=‖ui​n‖1,t≥0.\|u(t)\|_{1}=M:=\|u^{in}\|_{1}\ ,\qquad t\geq 0\ .

In particular, (u⁡(t),v⁡(t),w⁡(t))∈ℐM,θ(u(t),v(t),w(t))\in\mathcal{I}_{M,\theta} for all t≥0t\geq 0. Furthermore,

u∈C⁡((0,∞),W3,ℬ2​(Ω))∩C1​((0,∞),L3​(Ω)).u\in C((0,\infty);W_{3,\mathcal{B}}^{2}(\Omega))\cap C^{1}((0,\infty);L_{3}(\Omega))\ .

Several approaches may be used to deal with the well-posedness of (1.4)-(1.5). Since (1.4b) can be solved explicitly to find vv in terms of uu, one possibility would be to solve the parabolic system (1.4a)-(1.4c)-(1.4d)-(1.5) with a source term which is nonlocal with respect to time. However, since an abstract theory is developed in [2] to handle systems coupling parabolic equations and ordinary differential equations, we rather follow this route which provides the local well-posedness of (1.4)-(1.5) in W31​(Ω)W_{3}^{1}(\Omega) and may cope as well with nonlinear reaction terms in (1.4b) or (1.4c). The parabolic regularising effects of both (1.4a) and (1.4c) are then used to prove that it is actually a strong solution for positive times. Several estimates are next needed to prove that the solution is global, the positivity of ε\varepsilon being of utmost importance already in Lemma 2.3.

Having established the global well-posedness of (1.4)-(1.5), we next turn to qualitative information on the dynamics of (1.4)-(1.5) which is the main goal of this paper. We first study the boundedness of solutions, thereby extending [23, Theorem 1.2] to (1.4)-(1.5) in an arbitrary domain Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}.

Theorem 1.2.

Let θ∈(5/6,1)\theta\in(5/6,1) and consider initial conditions (ui​n,vi​n,wi​n)∈ℐM,θ(u^{in},v^{in},w^{in})\in\mathcal{I}_{M,\theta}. We denote the corresponding solution to (1.4)-(1.5) given by Theorem 1.1 by (u,v,w)(u,v,w).

  • (a)

    Assume further that M=‖ui​n‖1∈(0,4​π​D)M=\|u^{in}\|_{1}\in(0,4\pi D). Then

    (1.15) supt≥0{‖u⁡(t)‖∞+‖v⁡(t)‖∞+‖w⁡(t)‖W∞1}<∞.\sup_{t\geq 0}\left\{\|u(t)\|_{\infty}+\|v(t)\|_{\infty}+\|w(t)\|_{W_{\infty}^{1}}\right\}<\infty\ .

    Assume further that Ω\Omega is the ball Br​(0)B_{r}(0) of radius r>0r>0 centered at x=0x=0, (ui​n,vi​n,wi​n)(u^{in},v^{in},w^{in}) are radially symmetric, and M=‖ui​n‖1∈(0,8​π​D)M=\|u^{in}\|_{1}\in(0,8\pi D). Then (1.15) also holds true.

The proof of Theorem 1.2 (a) relies on the properties of the Liapunov functional ℰ\mathcal{E} (defined in (1.7b)) which are derived from the properties of ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0} (defined in (1.7a)) [9, 17]. The main observation is that, when (u,w)(u,w) belongs to the set 𝒜M\mathcal{A}_{M} defined in (1.9) and M∈(0,4​π​D)M\in(0,4\pi D), it follows from the Moser-Trudinger inequality [8] that

ℰ0​(u,w)≥4​π​D−M8​π​‖∇w‖22+δ2​‖w‖22−b\mathcal{E}_{0}(u,w)\geq\frac{4\pi D-M}{8\pi}\|\nabla w\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{\delta}{2}\|w\|_{2}^{2}-b

for some constant b≥0b\geq 0 which depends only on Ω\Omega, DD, δ\delta, MM, and ‖w‖1\|w\|_{1}. Therefore, an upper bound on ℰ0​(u,w)\mathcal{E}_{0}(u,w) entails an estimate on the W21W_{2}^{1}-norm of ww which, in turn, allows us to derive further estimates and deduce the boundedness of the solution. Similar arguments are used to prove Theorem 1.2 (b).

The final result deals with the unboundedness of some solutions provided ‖ui​n‖1\|u^{in}\|_{1} is large enough.

Theorem 1.3.

Let θ∈(5/6,1)\theta\in(5/6,1).

  • (a)

    Given M∈(4​π​D,∞)∖4​π​D​ℕM\in(4\pi D,\infty)\setminus 4\pi D\mathbb{N}, there are non-negative functions (ui​n,vi​n,wi​n)∈ℐM,θ(u^{in},v^{in},w^{in})\in\mathcal{I}_{M,\theta} for which the corresponding solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) to (1.4)-(1.5) given by Theorem 1.1 satisfies

    (1.16) lim supt→∞‖u⁡(t)‖∞=∞.\limsup_{t\to\infty}\|u(t)\|_{\infty}=\infty\ .

Given M∈(8​π​D,∞)M\in(8\pi D,\infty), there are non-negative radially symmetric functions (ui​n,vi​n,wi​n)∈ℐM,θ(u^{in},v^{in},w^{in})\in\mathcal{I}_{M,\theta} for which the corresponding solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) to (1.4)-(1.5) given by Theorem 1.1 satisfies (1.16).

On the one hand, Theorem 1.3 extends [23, Theorem 1.3] to (1.4)-(1.5) in an arbitrary domain Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} and, when Ω\Omega is a ball and the initial data are radially symmetric, applying the same approach to (1.1) is likely to provide an alternative proof of [23, Theorem 1.3]. It however only gives the unboundedness of the solution, while [23, Theorem 1.3] guarantees an exponential growth of the L∞L_{\infty}-norm of uu. On the other hand, Theorem 1.3 is also a consequence of the availability of a Liapunov functional and its properties, the latter being established in [10, 11, 13]. Roughly speaking, the proof of Theorem 1.3 involves three steps and proceeds along the lines of [13]. We first show that, given a solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) to (1.4)-(1.5) such that u∈L∞​((0,∞)×Ω)u\in L_{\infty}((0,\infty)\times\Omega), then there are a sequence (tk)k≥1(t_{k})_{k\geq 1}, tk→∞t_{k}\to\infty, of positive real numbers and a stationary solution (u∗,v∗,w∗)(u_{*},v_{*},w_{*}) to (1.4) such that

(1.17) ℰ⁡(u∗,v∗,w∗)≤lim infk→∞ℰ⁡(u⁡(tk),v⁡(tk),w⁡(tk)).\mathcal{E}(u_{*},v_{*},w_{*})\leq\liminf_{k\to\infty}\mathcal{E}(u(t_{k}),v(t_{k}),w(t_{k}))\ .

It next follows from [13, Lemma 3.5] that there is μM≥0\mu_{M}\geq 0 depending only on the parameters in (1.4) and MM such that

(1.18) ℰ⁡(u∗,v∗,w∗)≥−μM.\mathcal{E}(u_{*},v_{*},w_{*})\geq-\mu_{M}\ .

It now readily follows from (1.17), (1.18), and the fact that ℰ\mathcal{E} is a Liapunov functional that, if ℰ⁡(ui​n,vi​n,wi​n)<−μM\mathcal{E}(u^{in},v^{in},w^{in})<-\mu_{M}, then (u,v,w)(u,v,w) cannot be bounded. The last step is to check that such initial conditions exist, but this is again a consequence of the analysis performed in [10, 11, 13].

2. Global existence

2.1. Local existence

We begin with the local existence of solutions to (1.4)-(1.5) which is a consequence of the well-posedness theory developped in [2] for partially diffusive systems.

Proposition 2.1.

when δ​ε=1\delta\varepsilon=1.

Since z​e−z≤1/eze^{-z}\leq 1/e for z≥0z\geq 0, the upper bound (3.3) readily follows from (3.5). ∎

We next turn to the availability of a Liapunov function and recall that ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0} and ℰ\mathcal{E} are defined by

3.2. Time-independent estimates

As in [7, 9, 17], we exploit the structure of the Liapunov functional ℰ\mathcal{E} and first show that it is bounded from below as soon as MM is suitably small. To this end, we first recall the following consequence of the Moser-Trudinger inequality [8, Proposition 2.3], see [9, Corollary 2.6].

3.3. Stabilization

Another useful consequence of the availability of a Liapunov functional is the stabilization of bounded solutions; that is, any cluster point as t→∞t\to\infty of a bounded solution to (1.4)-(1.5) is a stationary solution to (1.4). Not only does this information provide better insight into the dynamics of solutions to (1.4)-(1.5) when ‖ui​n‖1<4​π​D\|u^{in}\|_{1}<4\pi D, since solutions are known to be bounded in that case by Theorem 1.2, but it is also an important step in the construction of unbounded solutions to be performed in Section 4. This fact has already been observed in [9] and used for similar purposes in [10, 11, 13].

4. Unbounded solutions

This section is devoted to the proof of Theorem 1.3 which is somewhat a direct consequence of the analysis performed in [10, 11, 13]. The main step is actually to recast the problem in a way suitable to apply results from [13].

Given M>0M>0, we define the set 𝒮M\mathcal{S}_{M} as follows: (u,v,w)∈𝒮M(u,v,w)\in\mathcal{S}_{M} if

5. Related models

To finish with, we just point out in an informal way that the related models (1.1) and (1.3) also have a Liapunov functional which is closely related to that of (1.4). Specifically, the functional ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0} defined by (1.7a) is a Liapunov functional for (1.1) and, if (u,v,w)(u,v,w) is a solution to (1.1), then

dd​tℰ0(u,w)=−∫Ωu|∇(lnu−w)|2dx−D∥∇∂tw∥22.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathcal{E}_{0}(u,w)=-\int_{\Omega}u|\nabla(\ln{u}-w)|^{2}\ \mathrm{d}x-D\|\nabla\partial_{t}w\|_{2}^{2}\ .

In the same vein, ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0} is also a Liapunov functional for (1.3) and, if (u,v,w)(u,v,w) is a solution to (1.3), then

dd​tℰ0(u,w)=−∫Ωu|∇(lnu−w)|2dx−νε(D∥∇∂tw∥22+δ∥∂tw∥22).\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathcal{E}_{0}(u,w)=-\int_{\Omega}u|\nabla(\ln{u}-w)|^{2}\ \mathrm{d}x-\nu\varepsilon\left(D\|\nabla\partial_{t}w\|_{2}^{2}+\delta\|\partial_{t}w\|_{2}^{2}\right)\ .

It is then likely that the analysis performed for (1.4) adapts to (1.1) and (1.3), possibly with slightly different statements for (1.1). Indeed, Proposition 4.1 (b) is only valid for M∈(8​π​D,∞)∖8​π​D​ℕM\in(8\pi D,\infty)\setminus 8\pi D\mathbb{N} in that case, see [11, Lemma 3].
